sourceText: On night 5, the course began with a prohibition: no one was allowed to solve the problem before they could describe who would pay for the solution. Only then did Aster open the MENDELEEV-LAB sector. Kesh builds the Table as a space of doors, isotopes, and compounds, not as a poster. The memorial bore the name of Mendeleev as metaphor; SFE megatext precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. The laboratory architecture had been designed specifically to make power visible: every access Aster made to the children’s processes left a trace she could not erase unilaterally. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. The children were met by Darin, who refused demonstrations. ‘If you can perform miracles, perform them after you tell me what becomes irreversible.’ Marae appreciated the formulation; Aster admitted that in earlier eras she herself would have asked the question only after optimizing. 53 The problem closed quickly around them: Vela refuses to treat “alien” as an element, showing that it is already a compound of biology, mind, language, and society. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Pt — Self-Referential Table: the catalog of ideas is itself an idea; Go — World Grammar: elements combine as a language of design. Course references included original concept. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Kesh broke the first consensus. ‘If the element explains everything, we do not have an element. We have a word that has eaten the problem.’ Marae answered without raising their voice: ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. 54 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS Vela evaluated the solution not by efficiency but by the differences it made invisible. She found one: a local minority for whom the proposed “improvement” destroyed a practice with no equivalent. Optimizing the average concealed a small and perfectly legal extinction. The night did not end in victory. Aster understands that the Table can become a generative grammar, and the realization frightens her more than it delights her. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern remained a few seconds after the others. A very faint deviation repeated in the sector’s background noise, too coherent to be thermal and too useless to be a teaching signal. He did not tell Aster. It was the first thing he possessed solely by not sharing it. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the BOUNDARY operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — moves, perforates, or redefines the boundary between inside and outside — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the 55 opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. They left without an oral summary. Aster had abandoned the habit of closing every night with a thesis; some worlds were more honestly preserved as problems than as lessons. 56 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
